en: The fourth chapter.
Great men do not desire even in their dreams to practice yoga, nor do they seize the hand [of a maiden] in marriage; they become lords of the earth by name alone. (4.1)
In a royal lineage, even though it is vast, one who causes all mountains to tremble is surely born,
like the tusk resembling Pṛthu in the mouth of the Lord of the Gaṇas.
Then, from that Puṣpabhūti—the best of the twice-born—he took up a treasury at his own will, like the lotus of the navel from the lotus-eyed Lord Viṣṇu;
like a collection of jewels preceded by Lakṣmī from the ocean;
like the host of planets—consisting mostly of Jupiter, Mercury, Venus, the Moon, the Sun, and Mars—from their place of rising.
From him emerged a royal lineage, capable of bearing the great burden like the ocean through the power of Sagara, and endowed with invincible strength like the Harivaṃśa from Sūra;
from whom arose lineages of subjects pure in their undecayed dharma, as if from the Kṛta age itself.

Like rays from a treasury of splendor that have pervaded the world with their majesty, like mountains from the preeminent of mountains that have filled the quarters of space with their physical forms,
and like the elephants of the directions from the hand of Brahmā who are capable of supporting the earth;
Like clouds rising from the onset of the rainy season to drink up the oceans,
like wish-fulfilling trees (*kalpataru*) from the Nandana grove that grant the fruits of one's desires,
and like the various forms of Viśvarūpa from Śrīdhara who is the refuge of all beings— kings were born.

And while they were thus arising in succession, there appeared a sovereign of kings named Prabhākaravardhana— also renowned by the secondary name Pratāpaśīla— who was a lion to the Hūṇa deer, a fever to the king of the Sindhus, a wakefulness to the Gūrjaras, a virulent consumption for the elephants that were the Gandhāra kings, a thief of the skill of the Lāṭas, and an axe to the creeper of the fortune of the Mālavas.
He who, at the very moment of his consecration, cast away riches like impurities clinging to the limbs of royalty;
he who felt no shame even for life itself—which, though belonging to another, was held as dear as a coward’s treasure and grasped like a blade of grass at the front of battle;

he who, in the midst of assemblies before his enemies in the heat of combat, was pained by his own reflection in the polished sword held in his hand, as if it were a rival companion; and he, a man of pride, who was distressed in his mind by the bow that bent even before him.
He bore the royal fortune with such immobility that it was as if it were fixed by the stakes, spikes, and bolts of the weapons of countless enemies held within him;

and he divided the earth into many portions for the use of his servants by means of vast military routes that leveled across all directions the ridges, hollows, thickets, forests, trees, grass, shrubs, anthills, mountains, and jungles.
And his majesty, though belonging to himself, scorched even those who had not yet tasted the desire for battle— driving back all enemies as if they were strangers;
he whose nature was like fire within their hearts and like water within the hollows of their eyes.
He was composed of wind in his exhalations,
composed of earth in his limbs, and composed of space in his emptiness.
His majesty was seen as if embodied, composed of the five great elements, within the harems of his vanquished vassals;
and in the presence of his jewel-like servants, he appeared like the goddess Lakṣmī herself reflected in their forms.
Furthermore, by the fire of his majesty, there arose prosperity (*bhūti*).
Success comes through the heat of valor;
the lineage flourishes by the water of the sword’s edge;
and manly effort is proclaimed through the mouths of weapon-wounds.
The scar from the bowstring became a place for his hand to rest;

and he regarded enmity as a gift, conflict as a favor, the onset of battle as a great festival, an enemy as the discovery of a treasure, an abundance of foes as prosperity, a challenge to combat as the granting of a boon, the fall of Skanda upon him as the increase of fortune, and the descent of a weapon’s blow as the taste of a shower of wealth.
Under that king, the Kṛta Yuga seemed to have sprouted forth as it were through the dense clusters of sacrificial posts;
Kali seemed to have fled away due to the smoke of sacrifices spreading toward the quarters of the sky;
and heaven seemed to have descended upon the earth with its celestial abodes complete with the ocean.
It seemed as if it were sprouted with dharma by the white banners fluttering atop the peaks of its celestial abodes;
as if it had given birth to villages through the vast assembly halls, alms-houses, fore-chambers, and pavilions constructed outside;
and as if it were shattered by Mount Meru through its opulences consisting of every utensil made of gold.
It was as if his fortune had borne fruit through the water-pots offered by the twice-born;
and even in another birth, he was accompanied by a virtuous wife like Pārvatī to Śaṅkara, or by Lakṣmī, who holds the hearts of all people, to the Teacher of the World.
With her pupils quivering, she was like Rohiṇī to the Moon;
like the intellect of Prajāpati, the mother of all beings;
and like the Gaṅgā born from the lineage of great mountains to the Lord of Rivers.
She was as skilled in following his mind as a female swan follows a royal swan;
her feet were honored by all the world like the three Vedas are the refuge of Dharma;
she never left his side day or night like Arundhatī beside the Great Sage; and in her movements, she was like a flock of swans.
She was like the cuckoo in her speech, like the ruddy goose in her love for her husband,
and like the rainy season in the swelling of her breasts.
She was like wine in her amorous graces,
like a treasure-trove in her accumulations of wealth,
and like a shower of gold in her favors.
Like the lotus in the gathering of its sheaths,
like the flower in the yielding of its fruit, and like the twilight in its state of being worthy of worship;
She was like the moon in her lack of heat,
like a mirror in her capacity to reflect every living being,
and like the ocean in her knowledge of the minds of others.
She was like the Supreme Self in her pervasive movements,
like memory in her virtuous actions,
and like honey in her conversations.
She was like nectar to those who thirsted,
like rain to her servants,
and like bliss to her friends.
She was like a cane-staff among her elders,
like the increase of lineage for her graceful charms,
and like the purification through penance for her womanhood.
She was like the fulfillment of the command of the god of love,
like the awakening of beauty,
and like the increase of fortune for Rati.
Like the fulfillment of a desire for loveliness, like the attainment of fate for beauty, like the birth of a lineage for affection;
Like the attainment of a boon for good fortune, like the birthplace of loveliness,
like the final consummation of beauty.
Like the very extension of youth,
like a cloudless rain of wit,
like the complete wiping away of misfortune for Fortune;
She was like the nourishment of fame for virtuous conduct,
like the satisfaction of the heart for righteousness,
and like the creation of the atoms of good fortune by the Lord of Creatures.
Like the tranquility of tranquility itself,
like the discipline of discipline itself,
like the nobility of nobility itself.
Here, there is restraint even for self-restraint, fortitude even for steadfastness,
and even confusion for delusion.
The chief queen named Yaśomatī was the ground of his life, affection, trust, righteousness, and happiness;
she shone upon his breast like the goddess Lakṣmī upon the chest of the Conqueror of Naraka.
Furthermore, by his very nature, that king was a devotee of the Sun.

Every day at sunrise, having bathed, wearing white silk garments, and with his head covered by a white cloth, he stood upon the ground on his two knees facing the east; in a mandala smeared with saffron paste, he offered an *arghya* oblation using a cluster of red lotuses placed in a sacred vessel of ruby—
lotuses as red as the sun itself, as if they were his own heart.

For the sake of offspring, the virtuous Ajapaccha muttered his prayers at dawn, at midday, and at the close of day; with a mind intent on his goal and great effort, he was constantly chanting the mantra known as the *Ādityahṛdaya*.
For the minds of the deities are subject to the entreaties of their devotees.
Thus, once during the summer season, the king happened to fall asleep upon the roof of a palace that was white as nectar, brightened by the rays of the moon.
And on his left side, on the second couch, Queen Yaśomatī lay;
as the night was almost spent,
when the beauty of the stars was being eclipsed by the approaching hour of dawn, and the lord of the stars was about to set, his luster fading away.
While the dew was dripping, as cool as the perspiration of the moon-born upon touching the night-lotuses that bloom at his touch;

while the lamps of the inner apartments were swaying as if intoxicated, having been struck by the breaths of women sleeping in the intoxication of wine and having thereby transferred their own languor to them;

and while the king’s feet seemed to be massaged by the stars reflected in his spotless new garments, as if those stars had extended their limbs with full confidence, offering themselves like celestial maidens fragrant with honey.

While her husband was being fanned by the beauty of his face with the breaths from his nostrils— as if by the wind from a palm-leaf fan held in his own lotus-like hand— and while he was graced by the reflection of the moon’s orb upon the surface of his spotless cheeks, which appeared like a crest of white flowers hanging down from the seizing of hair during amorous play,
Queen Yaśomatī suddenly cried out, "Noble Lord!"

"Save me! Save me! she cried out, her slender body trembling as if she were calling to her attendants with the tinkling of her ornaments; then, as if scorched in both ears by that sound of "Save me"—a cry never heard before on all the earth, let alone from the mouth of the Queen—the King instantly abandoned his sleep. And from the side of his head, he parted the night as it were with a bright-edged sword drawn by his right hand, which trembled with rage, appearing like a blue lotus emerging from his ear.
Waving with the sprout-like palm of his left hand an upper garment that acted as a spatial divider like the sky itself,

he was resplendent with a golden bracelet that had slipped from his hand by the force of its movement and was spinning through the quarters like a heart searching for the cause of its fear; meanwhile,
the palace trembled under the weight of his left foot as it was swiftly lowered and set down.
He was resplendent with a necklace that had fallen before him, severed as it came within the range of his sword’s edge like a fragment of the moon’s rays;
with eyes exceedingly red from both sleep and anger—as if stained by the juice of betel lingering from Lakṣmī’s kisses—he was flushing the horizons at their borders;
and with a triple-furrowed frown that bound together the darkness of night, he seemed once again to be turning back the three watches of the night, saying: “O Queen!”
Saying, "Do not be afraid! Do not be afraid! he sprang up with speed.
When he cast his eyes in all directions and saw nothing at all, he then asked her the cause of her fear.
Now, while the female watchmen were running away as if they were household deities,
When her attendants, who were sleeping nearby, had awakened,
and when the heart-trembling terror had subsided, she spoke: "Noble son,
I know that in a dream two young boys emerged from the orb of the divine sun."
Consisting of brilliance, they filled the quarters of the sky as if with the morning sun, making the world of living beings appear as if it were composed of lightning.
wearing crowns, wearing earrings, and wearing armlets;
Clad in armor, grasping weapons, and bathed in blood as red as Indragopaka insects, they stood there.
Being saluted by the entire world with uplifted faces and hands joined in añjali at their heads,
and followed by a single maiden who, like the moon’s form itself, seemed to have emerged from a ray of the *suṣumṇā* light, they descended to the surface of the earth.
"And while I was lamenting, those two began to tear open my belly with a weapon and enter it.
But I woke up, O Āryaputra, crying out and with a trembling heart."

And at this very moment in the sequence of time, the morning conch resounded at the gateway, as if proclaiming the fruit of the dream—the first address of royal fortune. The kettledrums thundered loudly, as if announcing auspicious prosperity for the king. And the morning drum, struck by its mallet, rang out as if from joy.
The loud cries of "Victory! Victory! were heard from those reciting auspicious hymns of awakening.
And in the stable of the king’s favorite horses, a man who had slowly risen from sleep saw before him his steeds emitting sweet neighs;
as he scattered upon them green barley, emerald-hued and dripping with sprays of frost-moistened water, he recited from the *Vaktra* and *Aparavaktra* meters:
“In this world, the arrival of good fortune is clearly indicated by signs: a treasure by the transformation of a tree, and a precious gem by its radiant luster. (4.3)
Like the dawn heralding the sun, or the wind heralding the arrival of rain, so does the appearance of a preceding omen foretell for men fortune or misfortune alike. (4.4)
But the king, hearing this, with a heart full of joy, said to her: "Queen, you despond at a time for rejoicing;
the blessings of your elders have borne fruit."
Our wishes are fulfilled;
you are protected by the family deities;
the Blessed One, the Sun-garlanded one, is pleased with you.
"Before long, she will gladden you by obtaining three children of exceeding virtue.
Having descended, she performed the rites as they were prescribed.
Yaśomatī, too, was delighted by those words of her husband.
Then, after some time had passed, Prince Rājyavardhana was first conceived in the womb of Queen Yaśomatī.
Even while he remained in the womb, his mother assumed a paleness as if from his own glory;
and as if exhausted by the weight of his virtues, she was unable to bear her body.
As if satiated by the nectar-like essence of the radiance spreading from her beauty, she turned her face away from food.
Gradually becoming languid due to her growing pregnancy, she was led with great difficulty to pay her respects, even though restrained by her elders, as her friends supported her by the hand.
As she rested, she appeared like a stone statue leaning against the pillars and walls nearby.
She was unable to lift her feet, which were as if surrounded by bees clinging out of greed for the lotuses;
and she wandered very slowly, as if being gathered up by the palace swans that had settled upon the rays of her toenails out of greed for lotus stalks.
Even toward her own reflections falling upon the jeweled walls, she extended her lotus-hand out of a desire to grasp them.
How much more so among her friends? She even desired to grasp the radiance of the ruby pillars, let alone the house-creepers.
She was incapable even of directing the household duties, let alone performing them;
as for her pair of feet, exhausted by the weight of her anklets, they could not endure ascending the palace even in thought.
She was unable to lift even her limbs, let alone her ornaments;
though she thought of climbing the pleasure-mountain, her breasts trembled with fear;
and even when rising to greet [her husband], she supported herself as if out of pride upon the tips of her budding hands placed on the peaks of both knees, held up by her pregnancy.

Day after day, with her face turned downward, she beheld her embryo with great joy; her lotus-like face seemed to have entered within her out of an eager longing to see her offspring, as it was reflected upon the surface of her breasts.
She bore a splendor that appeared doubled, for she held her son within her womb and her husband within her heart.
Having relinquished her body from the lap of her friends, she placed her feet upon the laps of her female attendants, but upon the heads of her co-wives.

And when the tenth month had arrived, she gave birth to Prince Rajyavardhana— a being fashioned as if from the atoms of Indra’s thunderbolt to inspire devotion in all the kings of the earth, equipped with the ornaments of Śeṣa’s circle of hoods to bear the weight of the three worlds, and constructed as if from the limbs of the world-elephants to cause the trembling of every mountain.

And upon his birth, the subjects were born as if made of dance, filled with joy; for one month, the king held a great festival that was like a single day— a celebration enchanting the world of mortals intoxicated with delight, resonant with the sound of countless filled conchs, sharp with the noise of hundreds of beaten drums, and filling the earth to its depths with the deep rumbling of kettledrums.

Then, after some time had passed, when the sky was filled with budding *kandali* plants, when the *kadamba* trees were covered in buds, when the clumps of *tokma* grass had grown, when the lotuses were still closed, and when the hearts of the *cātaka* birds were blooming while the swans remained silent— in that month, joy arose simultaneously in the heart and in the womb of Queen Yashomatī, just as it did in Devakī when the Discus-bearer [Kṛṣṇa] was born.

Gradually, as if embraced by the accumulated merit of all living beings, her slender frame once again became pale. With the onset of pregnancy, her two jar-like breasts, their beautiful nipples darkening at their tips, appeared upon her chest as if sealed shut to prevent anyone from drinking their contents. Her gaze, long, tender, and bright, assumed a sweetness like a river of milk placed upon her face for the sake of providing nourishment for her infant.
Her gait became slow and languid simply through the weight of her limbs, which were presided over by a multitude of every auspicious sign.

As she moved very slowly, it seemed as though the earth itself began its preliminary service, having grasped her sprout-like feet under the guise of her reflection submerged in the spotless jeweled pavement.

As she lay upon her couch for the day, she appeared like Lakṣmī herself, awaiting the time of her delivery, her image reflected in the surface of her stainless cheeks within the decorative leaf-patterns of the headboard.

On nights when she had ascended to the top of the palace roof, the orb of the moon was seen reflected upon her breast, which was exposed by her loosened garment as she suffered the pangs of pregnancy; it appeared like a white parasol being held over her womb by some unseen hand.

Even the maidservants holding yak-tail fans painted on the variegated walls of her bedchamber began to wave them as she slept. In her dreams, she was consecrated with water from lotus-leaf cups held in the trunks of the four elephants of the quarters; and as she awoke, the attendants carved upon the pillars of the moon-chamber seemed to rise up.
Even then, they repeatedly raised shouts of victory;
when the attendants were being summoned, bodiless voices issued forth saying, "Command them!";
and even during play, he could not tolerate the breaking of his commands.
Moreover, she felt a desire to bathe in the waters of all four great oceans combined;

her heart longed to wander through the interiors of forest-creeper bowers on the shore and along the sandy banks; and even in matters of urgent business, her creeper-like brow moved with graceful deliberation.
Even though jeweled mirrors were at hand, he had a longing to behold his face in the polished surface of a sword-blade;
the sounds of bows, which were unpleasant to the ears of women and thus set aside, caused him distress when heard; and his eye took delight in lions within their cages.
Even in bowing before her guru, her head seemed as if paralyzed and could only with great effort be made to incline.

Her friends, their eyes wide with joy, brightened the palace as if they were anticipating the great festival of her imminent delivery; they incessantly showered the place with a rain of blooming white, red, and blue lotuses and water-lily petals, as if creating a perpetual store of protective offerings.
They did not leave his side for even a moment in any direction;
and great physicians, seated in places befitting themselves and bearing various medicinal herbs like mountains supporting the earth, provided stability to the ground.
Like the hearts of the oceans arrived together with Lakṣmī, excellent jewels were fastened in the knots of their neck-threads.

Then, when the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūlīya had arrived, on the twelfth day of the dark fortnight, as the time of evening had passed and the youth of the night was about to ascend, a sudden clamor arose among the women in the inner apartments. Rushing out in haste, Supātrā— the daughter of Yaśovatī’s nurse and no less dear to her than her own heart— fell at the king’s feet and cried, “O Lord!...”
"Congratulations on your increase of fortune by the birth of a second son! saying this, she took up a vessel full of grain.
At that very moment, there arrived the king's most esteemed astrologer, who had correctly predicted hundreds of events beyond the senses and had demonstrated his supernatural power.

An astrologer named Tāraka— who had mastered all the compendiums of planetary conjunctions, was honored and beneficial among all mathematicians, and possessed knowledge of the three periods of time— approached and addressed the King: "Your Majesty,

it is heard that Māndhātṛ indeed took birth on such a day, free from the affliction of all defects such as *vyatīpāta*, when all the planets were situated in their respective exaltations and at such a *lagna*."
From that time until now, in this interval, no other person has been born in this world who possesses such a yoga as this for the birth of a universal monarch (cakravartin).

This son is the foremost among the seven universal monarchs, the recipient of the great jewels which are the marks of a universal monarch, the protector of the seven oceans, the initiator of all seven sacrificial threads (saptatantu), and equal to the sun (saptasapti).
"Born of the God!"—
in the midst of this, even though not blown by anyone, conchs resounded with a loud and sweet tone;
and even without being struck, the consecration drum thundered with a sound as deep as the roar of the agitated ocean.
Even though they were unsounded, the auspicious musical instruments resounded;
the echo of the music wandered through the quarters of the sky like a drum proclaiming safety for all the worlds.
And the joyful horses, their manes and tails tossed about, neighed loudly with mouths praised by the mouthfuls of green dūrvā grass-blades they had seized with pride.
The elephants, as if dancing with their sprout-like trunks gracefully uplifted, trumpeted in a manner pleasing to the ear;
and for a moment, a divine breeze blew, fragrant with the scent of wine like the breath of Lakṣmī as she cast aside her discus-weapon.
In the temples of the sacrificers, the arrival of auspicious fortune was foretold by clusters of flames turning to the right.
The sacrificial fires blazed forth without fuel;
great treasures emerged from the surface of the earth, their jars beautiful with handles fashioned like chains of refined gold.
Under the guise of the echoes of beaten auspicious instruments, even the world-protectors in every direction raised a clamor of joy at this increase of fortune.
At that very moment, twice-born men dressed in white robes, with faces like Brahmā, appeared like the Lords of Creatures of the Kṛta Age for the sake of increasing the progeny;
the family priest stood before them like Dharma incarnate, holding in his hand water for peace and sacrificial fruits;
and the elder kinsmen who had arrived were seen like ancient established customs returned.

With faces tangled in masses of long, drooping beards and bodies darkened by the stain of thick layers of dirt, the throngs of prisoners released from their bonds ran about in agitation like the kinsmen of the fleeing Age of Kali;
the market streets, plundered by the people, appeared like the camp-lines of Unrighteousness having retreated at that moment.
Surrounded by groups of laughing, upturned-faced dwarfs and deaf men, the elderly nurses, crowded with many children, danced like the very goddesses of motherhood incarnate.

And there unfolded a great festival for the birth of a son, in which the established order of the royal court had vanished; the figure of the chamberlain was cast down; the staff-bearers were dismissed; entry into the inner apartments was granted without restriction; master and servant were on equal footing; the distinction between child and elder was obliterated; the refined and the uncultured were alike; it was difficult to discern who was intoxicated and who was sober; the dalliance and conversation of noble maidens and courtesans were indistinguishable; and the entire population of the capital joined in the dance.
Starting from the following day, [the women] arrived from all directions, as if the kingdoms of women had been surrendered,
as if the caverns of the asuras had been opened, and as if the inner apartments of Nārāyaṇa had overflowed.
Families descended to earth like those of the Apsarases;
attendants carried baskets filled with flower-garlands strewn with bathing-powders;
and vessels were filled with pieces of camphor as white as fragments of crystal stone.

There were vessels made of jewels, scented with saffron; ivory caskets white with sandalwood and bristling with rows of betel-nut slabs, their interiors thickly matted with a network of thin khadira-wood filaments softened by mango oil;
and *pāṭala* and *pāṭalaka* flowers, whose fragrance was being drunk by swarms of humming bees.

Thousands of the harems of the vassal lords were seen approaching the royal palace from all sides, dancing with their jeweled anklets jingling as they stamped their feet, followed by attendants carrying vessels of vermilion and vessels of fragrant powders, as well as small betel trees bearing hanging rolls of betel leaves.
Gradually, the festival unfolded: in one place, the king’s affection was celebrated by the dancing of a circle of ancient, modest sons of noble families who were unaccustomed to such performances;
in another, the king’s favorites were being dragged away by intoxicated, low-born maidservants while the monarch looked on with an inward smile;
and elsewhere, the lord of men laughed heartily as an elderly noble vassal, clinging to the neck of a procuress from the royal camp, danced with unrestrained abandon.
In one place, the elaborate schemes of secret amours among ministers were being hinted at by the songs of wicked slaves, whose names were known only to the king;
in another, public laughter was provoked by an old mendicant being embraced by a drunken female servant;
and elsewhere, there was a battle of foul speech commenced by insolent servants fiercely vying with one another.
In some places, the inner apartments were filled with female slaves who were being made to dance by force, dragged away from their homes by women;
[the city] was like a mountain with heaps of flowers,
and like a tavern with its wine-stalls.
It was like the Sanandana grove with the fragrances of *pārijātaka* flowers; like a misty morning with the dust of camphor; like a boisterous laugh with the sounds of drums;
and like the churning of the nectar with its great tumult.
He was like the *saṃvarta* fire within the circle of the *rāsa* dance,
as if covered in horripilation by the rays of the jewels in his ornaments, and as if adorned with a ceremonial turban-band by the sandalwood marks upon his forehead.
The festive joy was as if accompanied by echoes, as if possessed of sprouting shoots through the granting of favors;
like Kamboja horses with filigree garlands hanging from their necks, they seemed to be leaping forward.
With pupils as tremulous as those of deer taking flight,
like the sons of Sagara tearing up the earth with merciless blows of their feet using spades,
thousands of youths played there.
In some way, the earth endured the agitation caused by the feet of the cymbal-beaters and bards;
and as the princes of the protectors of the earth played, pearls burst forth from their ornaments due to their mutual collisions.
Furthermore, with the dust of vermilion, the shell of the cosmic egg became as if crimsoned with the blood of the newly born Hiraṇyagarbha.

The vault of the sky shone as if it were covered with thousands of sandbanks of the Mandākinī revealed by the clouds of fine cloth-powder. The days gleamed as if colored by the mass of filaments from the lotus of the Grandfather (Brahmā) shattered by the upheaval of the world, their sunlight turned tawny by the scattered dust of fragrant powders. The people stumbled over the heaps of pearls fallen from necklaces broken in the crush.

They were followed by musical instruments being played at various points: with the *aliṅgyaka* being struck very gently; with the sweet-sounding flute tinkling; with the *jhallarī* cymbals clanging; with the stringed *paṭahikā* drum being beaten; with the *lābu-vīṇā* gourd-lute being played without excessive noise; with the bronze *kāhalā* pipe resounding; and with the *tālīka* cymbals being struck in perfect unison.
At every step, their rhythmic tempo was followed as if by connoisseurs through the jingling sounds of their ornaments;
like cuckoos, they warbled with soft, sweet, and intoxicated warbling,
singing indecent verses of *rāsaka* dance that were nectar to the ears of libertines.
Wearing garlands of skulls,
with ear-ornaments like young shoots,
and marked with sandalwood tilakas.
Embracing the sun, as it were, with their creeper-like arms raised high and made resonant by rows of bracelets;
with bodies beautiful from the smearing of saffron, they bounded like young maidens of Kashmir;
and with large, dangling *kuraṇṭaka* flowers upon their heads hanging down to the curves of their hips, they seemed ablaze with the fire of passion.
With their facial features smeared with streaks of vermilion,
they were like rows of proclamatory tablets for Kandarpa, whose commands are irresistible;
dusted with camphor and fragrant powder scattered by their fists, they were like the carriage-roads for the wandering of youth’s desires.
Striking young men with garlands of loose-flowing flowers like female door-keepers of the great festival of youth;
shining with earrings of trembling leaves like creepers of the sandalwood tree of Love;
and resonant with the cries of swans in their graceful steps as they frolicked like waves of the ocean of the erotic sentiment.

Devoid of discrimination between what should and should not be said, like the play of children, their slender bodies were bristling with excitement at the deep sound of kettledrums; like *ketakī* flowers shedding their pollen, they shed tears;
and as if possessed, they were surrounded by throngs of kings.
Like affections, they captivated the heart; like songs, they kindled passion;
like nourishments, they produced joy.
As if intoxicating even intoxication itself,
as if coloring even passion itself, as if gladdening even bliss itself.
They seemed to make even the dance itself dance, to celebrate even the festival itself,
and in their sidelong glances, they seemed to drink with the shells of their outer corners of the eyes.

In their gestures of threat, they seemed to bind him with nooses of light from their fingernails; in their displays of anger, they seemed to strike him with the movements of their creeper-like eyebrows;
and in their affectionate conversations, they seemed to rain down all the aesthetic sentiments.
In the four walkways, courtesans danced as if scattering their charms;
elsewhere, forest deities seemed to appear, with spaces cleared by the staffs of guards and surrounded by groves of white parasols being held aloft.

Some wandered like celestial trees beneath the wish-fulfilling kalpavṛkṣas; some, with their hands clinging to long upper garments hanging from both shoulders, swayed as if mounted upon playful swings;
and some, with the waves of their silken scarves being torn by the tips of their golden armlets, were like rivers whose currents are parted by soaring cakravāka birds.

Some, with their wide side-glances turned toward the three-pronged crest-jewels caught in the bristles of their waving white chowries, resembled lakes where groves of blue lotuses are being pulled by swans;
others, with palace swans being sprinkled by droplets of sweat reddened by the lac falling from their moving feet,
were like moonlit nights when the lunar orb is being colored by the glow of twilight.

Some of the queens, who were like the snares of Love with their outstretched arms as nooses, shone forth having begun their dance; their faces were slightly contracted by the graceful movements of their bodices, which were adorned with golden girdles fastened around their necks.
And the earth, reddened on all sides by the flowing lac from the feet of the dancing host of women, seemed as if it were composed of passion itself.
With their radiant circles of breasts, the great festival appeared as if it were composed of auspicious jars.
With the tossing of their vine-like arms, the world of living beings shone as if made of lotus-fiber bracelets;
with their shimmering playful smiles, time was rendered as if composed of lightning;
and by the brilliance of their flickering glances, the days became as if filled with black antelopes.
With ear-ornaments of shimmering *śirīṣa* flower clusters, the sunlight became green-hued as if composed of parrot feathers;
with the tamāla leaves from loosened braids falling down, the sky appeared as if made of collyrium;
with uplifted sprout-like hands, the created beings seemed to be made of lotuses; and by the radiance of rubies and rainbows, the sunbeams shone as if they were made of peacock feathers.
The quarters of the sky resounded as if made of tiny bells due to the echoes of the clashing masses of ornaments;
even the elderly women were like those possessed by madness,
and even the most venerable elders, as if seized by a demon, felt no shame.
Even the learned forgot themselves as if intoxicated; they made even the minds of the sages tremble with the desire to bow down;
and the king gave away his entire possession.
In every direction, heaps of wealth were plundered by the people as if they were the treasuries of Kubera;
and while that great festival was thus proceeding, time gradually passed away once more.
And while the King had mustard seeds for protection placed upon his head,
his body was tawny-gold, as if from the sparks of the fire of his burgeoning majesty,
and his neck was adorned with a row of formidable tiger claws set in gold, as if manifesting his innate kṣatriya splendor.
With the sprout of pride budding within his heart,
he seemed to be slowly and gradually uttering the syllable *oṃ* of Truth through his first indistinct babblings;
with his charming smiles, like flowers, he attracted the hearts of his kinsmen as bees are drawn by blossoms.
His lotus-face was being adorned by the sprouts of playful smiles arising as if from the sprinkling of the spray of nectar from the jar-like breasts of his mother;
he was being protected by the assembly of women in the inner apartments as if by his own conduct, and guarded by the circle of ministers as if by a secret counsel.
He was being released by the circle of noble youths as if he were a virtuous deed;
he was being nurtured by his own will as if he were fame;
and he was situated within the cage of the weapons of the guardian men as if he were a cub of the king of beasts.
While Harṣa took five or six steps while holding onto the fingers of his nurse’s hand,

and Rājyavardhana was entering his sixth year, Queen Yaśomatī conceived the goddess Rājyaśrī, who was like the earth bearing the form of Nārāyaṇa. And when the days of her delivery were complete, she gave birth to one whose eyes had long, red stalks, like a lotus-plant in a lake.
She was like the autumn season with its sweet-voiced swans,
like the splendor of spring with its forest groves whose limbs are as delicate as flowers,
and like the heavens showering a stream of pure, great gold.
She was like the ocean shore showering a rain of jewels; she was like the crescent moon on the first day of the lunar fortnight, bringing joy to the eyes of all people;
she was like Śacī beholding Jayantī, worthy of being gazed upon by the thousand-eyed Indra.
Menā gave birth to a daughter who was sought after by all the kings, just as Gaurī was;

by her, the mother shone exceedingly with both sons, like a single-stringed necklace between two breasts. At this very time, however, Queen Yaśomatī’s brother brought forth a son about eight years of age, whose head was adorned with the sprouting, curved feathers of a young peacock and whose hair was bound by a streak of smoke from the fire of the roar of the wielder of the *khaṇḍaparaśu* (Śiva).
He was like the god Makaradhvaja reborn,
appearing as if he were a combined incarnation of Hari and Hara, with one half of his body darkened by an emerald earring and the other half whitened by the light of a three-pronged pearl ornament;
he wore a ring of flower-metal on his thick forearm, resembling the young son of Tāḍakā marked by the axe— the very weapon that had been blunted by the destruction of the Kṣatriyas under Paraśurāma.

He presented to the two princes an attendant named Bhaṇḍi, who was like a second Hiraṇyakaśipu having taken another birth—his curved coral sprouts were strung upon a necklace of necklaces, and his chest, hardened by its own firmness, bore the scars of Narasiṃha’s claws; even in childhood, he possessed great self-possession, appearing like the very seed of the essence of valor.
The king’s regard for him was equal to that for his two sons, just as the Lord’s third eye is equal to his other two.

The two princes also shone exceedingly, having been joined by that naturally skillful [minister], who captivated the hearts of all living beings, like the months of Madhu and Mādhava joined by the Malaya breeze.
In due course, growing up together with their other brother, the joy of the subjects, they entered their youth.

With firm thighs as pillars, broad forearms, long arms as bolts, and wide chests as door-panels, they were as delightful as tall palaces; like the layout of a great city, they became capable of providing refuge for all the world.
Then, like the moon and the sun, they were beautiful yet difficult to behold because their splendor overwhelmed the world with flashing rays of light;
like fire and wind, they were united as one, manifesting both brilliance and power;
and with bodies as firm as rock, they were as immovable as the Himalayas and the Vindhya mountains.
Like two great bulls fit for the Kṛta age;
like Aruṇa and Garuḍa, whose bodies were divided between the vehicles of Hari;
like Indra and Upendra, mounted upon the king of serpents and the king of birds;
Like Karṇa and Arjuna wearing earrings and crowns;
like the eastern and western quarters of the horizon whose purpose is to bring about the rise and setting of all luminous bodies;
and like two oceans that could not be contained within the narrow confines of the Kukuṭīraka cave due to their excessive magnitude, which was constricted by the barrier of the nearby shore.
Turning their backs on splendor, they loathed even its shadow;
they were ashamed even by the reflection of their own bodies clinging to their toenails;
and they found distress even at the breaking of a single hair.

Feeling ashamed even by the second parasol reflected in their crest-jewels, their ears pained at hearing the title "Lord" applied even to the Blessed Six-faced One (Kārttikeya), and their eyes distressed by seeing even a rival man reflected in their mirrors;
Even when joining their palms in salutation at twilight, their heads felt like a stake;
even by the bow held by the clouds, their hearts were made to tremble;
and even by painted kings who did not bow down, their feet were tormented with pain.
They held even the splendor of the sun in low esteem, as it was satisfied with only a limited orb;
they mocked even the ocean for having its majesty stolen away by a mountain;
and they censured even the wind, though it was powerful, for not engaging in combat.
Though fanned by the yak-tail whisks of even the Himavat mountains, they were scorched; though comforted by the conch shells of even the oceans, they were distressed;
and they could not endure even another lord of the four seas, namely Varuṇa.
They caused even those kings whose royal parasols had not been snatched away to lose their luster; they were gracious even toward the virtuous,
yet they poured forth sweetness from their mouths.

Bringing despondency even to those situated far away by the heat of their lineage of wicked kings; daily bearing palms blackened by the stains of sword-practice as if soiled by extinguishing the fire of the majesty of all rival monarchs;
and at times of exercise, conversing with the neighboring regions—those brides of the quarters—as if with firm bow-strings sounding like voices, O Rājyavardhana.
Thus, the names "Harṣa" and "Śarva" became manifest throughout the entire earth; in a very short time, their fame spread even to other continents.
On one occasion, having invited them and finished his meal, his father, remaining in private, spoke affectionately: "My children!"
The first limb of sovereignty is that good servants are difficult to find.
Generally, like atoms, the base, acting in concert, constitute a substance; yet, when made to dance by the king through the pleasure of play, the foolish lead him to the state of a peacock.
Like reflections entering a mirror, the *pallavikas* transmit their own nature [to others];
like dreams, the deceivers produce false perceptions through illusory appearances;
and like the symptoms of a fever, when indulged, they bring about madness through song, dance, and laughter.
Like thirsty *cātaka* birds, those of low birth cannot be captured; like fishermen, they seize the very intention as it flashes in the mind.
Like painters on a canvas in the sky, the singers paint their colorful designs;
like hunters, they pierce the heart with arrows.

Since these two sons of the King of Mālava, named Kumāragupta and Mādhavagupta— untouched by any of these aforementioned faults, pure, disciplined, courageous, and handsome— are like my own two arms, inseparable from my body, I have designated them as your attendants for your service. They have been tested by wise men and found to be free from all such blemishes.
"Over these two, you both must not behave like other attendants," he said,
and commanded the doorkeeper to summon them.
Before long, Rājyavardhana and Harṣa, their eyes fixed upon the entrance, entered together with the doorkeeper.
In front of him was his eldest son, eighteen years of age, neither too tall nor too short, who seemed to steady the earth—shaken by the passage of many kings—with his exceedingly heavy strides;

he shone with a pair of slender shanks that appeared as if they had emerged from his thighs, which were thick with flesh hardened by the constant practice of leaping, while the prominent knots of his knees were not visible;
and with his sides so carved as to reveal his leanness, he resembled Mount Mandara, wasted by the friction of Vasuki as he was whirled about by the impetuous force of the gods and demons.
He was characterized by a chest so exceedingly broad that it seemed to offer space for the boundless honors bestowed upon him by his master;
with the quiet and graceful movements of his long, hanging arms, he appeared as if crossing the difficult-to-traverse ocean of youth;

and his thick forearm was marked by the scar of a bowstring, which, dense with the mass of rays from the rubies on his left-hand bracelet, seemed like a sprout of the flame of his own majesty breaking forth.

He bore the radiance of the gem in his ear-ornament like the skin of a Ruru deer, reddish-brown and hanging down from the slope of his high shoulder, held there by the vow of taking up arms; he wore on his face—whose cheeks were filled with the reflections of the figures carved on the leaf-patterns of his high-set armlets—the moon itself, with Rohiṇī residing within his heart;
and with his downward-turned gaze, its pupils steady and unmoving, he seemed to be teaching humility to the clusters of lotuses that had raised their faces upward in their longing for Lakṣmī.
He wore upon his head an *amlātaka* flower as if it were the undying devotion of a master;
he manifested a humility that seemed bestowed by all the bows, terrified of having their ornaments broken, through the merciless [pressure of his grip];
and even in childhood, he shone with his senses conquered and restrained, like subdued enemies.
He followed the path of noble birth as if it were a beloved confidante;
though possessed of brilliance, he shone with a pleasing character like the sun with the moon within it;
and by his physical grace, he seemed to impart fragrance even to the mountains.

The joy you derive from the sight of Kumāragupta is as if you were selling him for his good fortune to the people; behind him was his younger brother, who, due to his extreme height and fair complexion, seemed like a moving mountain of realgar,
his head as if kissed by his heavy fame— which, desiring to go forth, had taken the guise of a modest crest of *mālatī* flowers.
He seemed to announce, by the joining of his eyebrows, the first sign of a long-awaited meeting between discipline and youth, which are naturally opposed to one another;
with extreme composure, he maintained a steady gaze that appeared like his devotion to his master fixed within his heart;

and his chest—cooled by the application of pure sandalwood paste and served as a pillow for his nearby necklace—was like a broad bed of moonstone slabs for the Goddess of Fortune, who was weary from her wanderings among endless vassal kings.

They beheld Mādhavagupta, who appeared as if displaying the eyes of deer, the bridge of his nose from boars, the foundation of his shoulders from buffaloes, the joints of his forearms from tigers, his prowess from lions, and his gait from elephants— all of whom, exhausted by the hunt, had offered him what seemed like bribes out of fear.

Having entered, they paid homage from afar, touching the earth with their four limbs and their heads. They took their appropriate places as indicated by the affectionate glance of the king. After standing there for a moment, the monarch commanded them: "From this day forward, you two must attend upon the princes."
“As Your Majesty commands,” replied Rājyavardhana and Harṣa, rising with their crowns touching the ground;
they both bowed before him as well as their father.

From that moment on, they never departed from the range of his vision for even a moment, like the opening and closing of his eyes; they stood facing him day and night like his own inhalation and exhalation; and they remained constantly by his side like his two arms.
Those two became the companions of the two princes.
Then Rājyaśrī also, her familiarity increasing day by day with skilled female friends in dancing, singing, and so forth, as well as in all the arts, grew up gradually;
in a limited number of days, she reached the prime of youth.

The stone slabs of all the kings fell upon her alone, like arrows upon a target; and the kings sought her hand with gifts of new garments and other offerings. Once, however, while the king was staying in the palace apartments of the inner harem, he heard an *āryā* verse being sung by a man stationed in the outer courtyard, which had come up in his turn: [The verse follows. The king, having heard it, reflected: "This is indeed a woman of noble character (*āryā*), for she does not even mention her own name. Then, at another time, when the king was seated in the assembly hall, that same man approached him and recited the verse again. The king asked, "By whom was this composed? He replied, "By a certain courtesan. The king said, "Bring her here. When she was brought, the king asked her, "Is this verse yours? She replied, "It is mine. The king said, "If it is yours, then compose one that will surpass it. She said, "If you grant me a boon," and the king granted her whatever she desired. She then spoke: [The second verse follows. The king, hearing this, was filled with wonder and said, "She is truly a woman of noble character (*āryā*). He then bestowed upon her a great reward and released her from her bondage. Thus, through the power of her virtue, she attained liberation from the cycle of rebirth. Therefore, one should always practice virtue. This concludes the story of the courtesan. Now, as for the story of the merchant’s son: once, in the city of Pāṭaliputra, there lived a merchant’s son named Guṇasāgara. He was handsome, virtuous, and beloved by the people. One day, while wandering about, he saw a certain woman who was exceedingly beautiful and possessed of every grace. He fell deeply in love with her. Desiring to win her, he sent messengers to her, but she would not accept him. He thought, "I must find some means to overcome her resistance. Then, having learned that she was devoted to the worship of the goddess Śrī, he went to the temple and began to perform service there. After some time, the woman came to the temple to worship the goddess. Seeing him, she was struck with desire and said to herself, "How can I win him over? She then devised a plan and sent a female messenger to him. The messenger went to the merchant’s son and said, "O noble sir, the lady desires to see you. He agreed, and they met. Thereupon, the woman took him to her home and enjoyed him according to her pleasure. From that time on, they lived together in constant intimacy. One day, the merchant’s son said to her, "My dear, I have no wealth; how shall I support you? She replied, "Do not worry; I possess much wealth. She then gave him a large sum of money and said, "Take this and live as you please. With that wealth, the merchant’s son lived in luxury. However, after some time, his wealth was exhausted. He then said to her, "My dear, my wealth is spent; what shall I do now? She replied, "Do not be distressed; I still have some savings. She gave him more money, and he continued to live with her. But eventually, his resources were completely depleted. He then said to her, "My dear, I am utterly destitute; I cannot remain here any longer. She replied, "If you must go, then take this final gift. She gave him a small amount of money and said, "With this, you may travel to another land. Taking that money, the merchant’s son departed. As he traveled along the road, he encountered a band of thieves. They seized him and stripped him of everything he had. He was left with nothing but his life. He wandered in despair until he reached a certain forest. There he saw a group of ascetics practicing penance. He approached them and related his misfortune. The ascetics, moved by compassion, took him under their care and taught him the way of spiritual discipline. Through their instruction, he abandoned all worldly attachments and became a perfected soul. Thus, through the power of his former merit and the guidance of the holy ones, he attained liberation. Therefore, one should always seek the company of the virtuous. This concludes the story of the merchant’s son. Now, as for the story of the king’s son: once, in the city of Ujjayinī, there lived a king named Mahendraprabha. He had a son named Candraprabha, who was handsome, brave, and wise. One day, the prince went out to hunt and entered a dense forest. There he saw
“Like a river that grows year by year, a daughter, as she increases, casts her father into the great whirlpool of anxiety at the time of her marriage, just as a river washes away its bank. (4.5)
Having heard this, he dismissed his attendants and spoke to the Great Queen standing by his side: “Queen, our child Rājyaśrī has reached the bloom of youth;
like her own excellence, the anxiety regarding her never departs from my heart for even a moment.”
At the very onset of youth, fathers become fuel for the fire of grief regarding their daughters.
The swelling of her breasts darkens my heart, as does the rising of clouds at the end of the day.

This righteous custom established by someone else is not pleasing to me: that children, born of one’s own body and cherished in one’s lap, should be taken away unexpectedly by strangers who have arrived uninvited.
These, indeed, are the very seats of suffering within this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

This is the all-conquering burning power of the fire of grief that, although the status of being a child is equal, causes the virtuous to suffer when a daughter is born. At the very moment of birth, the righteous offer water to their daughters with tears instead of [the ritual] *tarpaṇa*.
Out of fear of this, sages who have not taken wives and have abandoned dwelling in households lie down in empty forests.
For what conscious person indeed could endure the separation from their offspring?
Just as messengers from the suitors arrive one after another, so does anxiety, as if feeling ashamed, enter deeply into my wretched heart.
What can be done?
Nevertheless, those who have entered the household life must indeed follow the ways of the world.
Moreover, for the most part, even when other excellent qualities are present, the wise adhere primarily to noble lineage alone.

"The Maukhari dynasty, honored by the entire world like the footprint of Maheśvara placed upon the heads of the mountain-bearers, stands preeminent. Within that lineage, the eldest son of Avantivarman—who was like a tilaka-mark—named Grahavarman, has come to earth like the lord of the planets (the Sun) and, not inferior to his father in virtues, seeks her hand.

If your ladyship’s mind also consents, then I wish to give her to him. When her husband had spoken thus, the Queen, her heart overcome with affection for her daughter and her eyes filled with tears, replied: "Noble Lord!"
Indeed, mothers are no different from nurses for daughters, serving merely to nourish them;
however, their fathers are the ultimate authority regarding their giving away in marriage.
Moreover, the affection for a daughter exceeds that for a son by far, being distinguished by a particular intensity of compassion.
"The noble son alone knows how this may be so that it does not lead to enmity between us for as long as we live.

The king, having reached a firm decision regarding the giving away of his daughter, summoned his two sons and made them aware of the matter. On an auspicious day, he placed the formal document of the gift of his daughter into the hand of the chief messenger who had previously arrived to request the maiden on behalf of Grahavarman, in the presence of the entire royal court.

When he had departed with his purpose accomplished and filled with joy, and as the days of the wedding drew near, the entire populace was adorned with profuse gifts of betel, incense, and flowers; caravans of artisans were arriving from every region;
and a vast collection of implements was being brought in by the king’s men, gathered from all the villages.

It was a place where numerous royal tributes were being presented by the king’s doorkeepers; where the circle of beloved royal favorites gathered to welcome the assembly of kinsmen who had arrived upon invitation; and where auspicious drums resounded with sharp strikes from the tips of sticks brandished in the hands of leather-workers fierce with the intoxication of liquor.
The mortar, pestle, and stone slabs were being adorned with flour-pasted handprints;
the forecourts were filled by successions of wandering bards appearing from every direction, where an image of Indrāṇī was being installed;
and the master builders, honored with white flowers, unguents, and garments, were beginning to lay the foundation lines for the wedding altar.
The palace turrets, city gates, and rampart crests were being whitened by white-washers mounted on ladders, carrying baskets of lime and heaps of camphor;
the sprout-like hands of the people were being dyed by the surging floods of water used for washing vast quantities of crushed safflower;
and the courtyards were rippling with the movements of elephants and horses being inspected as dowry gifts.

The courtyard was filled with the sounds of the rhythmic clanging of goldsmiths' hammers as they fashioned gold, while the assembly of astrologers engaged in calculation determined the auspicious moment for the wedding; meanwhile, a multitude of pleasure ponds were being filled by crocodile-mouthed conduits discharging fragrant water.
The place was crowded with plasterers busy applying thick coatings of sand and thorny lime-paste to freshly heated walls;
it was filled with circles of clever painters sketching auspicious murals,
and groups of modelers fashioning clay figures of fish, tortoises, sea-monsters, coconut trees, plantain trees, and betel-nut palms.

And by the kings themselves, who had girded their loins and were busily intent on accomplishing the excellence of the tasks assigned by their master; who were smoothing the floors of vermilion-paved courtyards;

and who were erecting the pillars of the wedding dais—pillars upon which fresh offerings were placed in their hands, which were stained crimson with lac-dye, and whose tops were marked with sprouts of mango and *aśoka* trees—the various activities were already underway.
And from sunrise, virtuous, fortunate, beautiful, well-attired, and chaste women entered,

their foreheads adorned with streaks of vermilion powder, singing auspicious hymns pleasing to the ear that contained the names of the bride’s and groom’s lineages; they decorated necklaces with their fingers smeared with various pigments and were skilled in painting variegated creepers and figures.

There were women adorning white water-jars and rows of cool sandalwood floors; coloring unopened buds of cotton-wool shoots and wedding bracelets bound with woolen threads; preparing body-unguents mixed with saffron paste thickened with ghee and *balāśana*, as well as face-pastes that enhance the excellence of beauty; and [preparing] *jātī* fruits mixed with *kakkola* and interspersed with shimmering, abundant fragments of crystal-like camphor.

It was filled on all sides by the wives of the neighboring vassals as they fashioned garlands of cloves; and it was graced by red cloths— being woven by elderly city matrons skilled in the creation of various patterns, already bound, and being dyed by washermen shining with their expertise in ritual propriety for the inner apartments— which were swayed by attendants clinging to both ends of the cloth in the shade.

It was covered on all sides by garments being dried and already dry, their fresh beauty enhanced by the crooked movements of those working with them; by others beginning to smear themselves with patches of saffron paste; by others whose fragile upper robes were being torn by slave-boys with upraised arms; and by clothes made of linen, coarse wool, silk, and fine muslin spun from saliva-like fibers, resembling the sloughs of snakes, as soft as the core of a tender plantain tree, so light they could be carried away by a breath and discernible only by touch—like thousands of rainbows flashing everywhere.
With couches being enveloped by swans in brilliant coverlets; with bodices being adorned with star-shaped pearls;

with countless thousands of silk ribbons being cut and fashioned through various methods; with canopies shining with fresh-dyed, delicate *dukūla* silks; with pavilions whose entire surfaces were covered without gaps by heaps of *stavaraka* cloths; and with [objects] being wrapped in variegated eye-cloths.
The royal palace became radiant with pillars, delightful, inspiring longing, and auspicious; meanwhile,
Queen Yaśomatī’s heart was agitated by the wedding festival— toward her husband with affection,
and toward her son-in-law with curiosity.
With affection toward his daughter, with courtesy toward the invited women, and with authority toward his attendants.
in moving about with the body,
in examining what has been done and what remains to be done with the eyes, and in joy during great festivals;
Though she was but one, she appeared as if divided into many.

The king, too— his delight in his son-in-law being increased by the successive births of daughters-in-law from his female camels and mares— performed everything himself along with his two sons, his affection for his daughter overflowing, even though he had attendants skilled in executing his commands who were intent on watching his every gesture.
And so, while that royal household was as if filled with no widowhood,
the world of living beings was as if becoming filled with auspiciousness, and the quarters of the sky were as if becoming filled with bards;

Thus it was when that royal family became as if free from widowhood, the world of the living became as if composed of auspiciousness, and the faces of the directions appeared as if filled with wandering minstrels.
When the atmosphere was as if composed of the sound of drums,
the attendants were as if composed of ornaments, and the entire creation appeared as if composed of kinsmen;
At a time that appeared as if composed of liberation,
while a great festival unfolded as if consisting of prosperity— like a treasure-trove of happiness,
like the fruit of birth, and like the culmination of merit—
While prosperity was like youth,
joy was like the status of crown prince,
and desire was like the moment of its fulfillment.
As if being counted by the fingers of the people, as if being gazed upon by the banners along the road,
and as if being welcomed by the echoes of auspicious musical instruments;
As if being summoned by astrologers,
as if being drawn forward by his desires,
and as if being embraced by the hearts of his bride’s companions, the day of the wedding arrived.
At dawn, the royal palace was cleared of all common folk by the doorkeepers and made secluded.

Then, the chief chamberlain, having entered the presence of the king, announced, "Your Majesty, a trusted messenger named Pārijātaka, a betel-bearer from the presence of the son-in-law, has arrived," and presented a handsome young man of his own appearance.
But the king, showing his respect from afar out of great regard for his son-in-law, asked: "My boy,
is Gṛhavarman well?"

Hearing that sound of the king’s command, he ran forward a few paces, extended his arms, and, being skilled in service, bowed his head to the ground for a long time; then rising, he announced: "O King, I honor you with my salutation according to your instructions. Knowing that he had come to announce the arrival of the son-in-law and having shown him hospitality, the king sent him back with this message: "Ensure that no fault arises from the passing of the marriage hour during the first watch of the night."
He sent [the messenger]. Then, when the day had come to a close, having transferred the splendor of the entire lotus forest as if onto the face of the bride,
and while the sun was turning crimson like a sprout at the foot of the Fortune of the wedding day;
As the pairs of *cakravāka* birds separated, as if ashamed by a love that had been eclipsed by the passion of the bride and groom;

as the glow of twilight, like a banner of good fortune, shimmered in the sky which possessed the delicate body of a red parrot; and as the darkness, variegated like the neck of a pigeon, began to cloud the faces of the quarters as if it were the dust raised by the arrival of the bridegroom’s procession.

When the host of luminaries was rising as if prepared to bring about the auspicious moment (the *lagna*), and the orb of the moon—the lord of stars—was being lifted by the mountain of sunrise like a marriage-auspicious jar, casting forth an ever-increasing white radiance; when the night had its darkness swallowed by the moonlight of the bride’s face;

and when the beds of night-lotuses, with their upturned faces, seemed to mock the moon for having risen in vain; then [he] arrived, accompanied by horses whose forelocks were tossed repeatedly with broad, quivering, reddish chowries that appeared like longings personified, their tips bristling with passion like sprouting shoots.
The quarters of the sky were filled by throngs of cavalrymen rushing through the city, their horses neighing as if offering a welcome to the ears of the elephants;
and by herds of powerful elephants, whose ears served as waving chowries, who were equipped with all their trappings of gold, who wore colorful housings, and who rang with the clanging of bells.
As if once again churning away the darkness dissolved by the rising moon,
he ascended toward the eastern quarter like the moon ascending the direction of Indra, his face adorned with a garland of stars;
while a clamor was raised before him by various birds warbling in diverse notes, like young springtime groves accompanied by cymbal-beating minstrels.
Making the entire world tawny with a mass of saffron cloth-powder, as if with the light of a circle of lamps fragrant from the sprinkling of scented oil;
with his head—its floral crest resting amidst a wreath of full-blown jasmine—seeming to laugh at the moonlit night of the autumnal full moon encircled by its halo;
and displaying the grace of a cross-strap fashioned from a garland of flowers, as if it were the bow of the flower-arrowed god of love snatched away after he had been conquered by his own beauty.

Charming with the sweet warbling of swarms of bees wandering in pride at the fragrance of its flowers, like the *pārijāta* tree brought down again to earth along with the Goddess Śrī, Grahavarmā approached; his heart drawn as if by curiosity to behold the face of his new bride, he seemed to fall forward with his face as he drew near.
The King, followed by the circle of monarchs, went out on foot from the palace gate to meet him as he arrived.

When he had entered and offered his salutations, Rājyavardhana embraced him firmly with outstretched arms, like Mādhava embracing Manmatha; then, having greeted Harṣa in due order, he took him by the hand and led him inside. There, he attended upon him with honors such as offering him a seat no different from his own.
And before long, the learned and beloved courtier of the king named Gambhīra, the foremost among the twice-born, said to Grahavarman:

"Dear friend, having obtained you, the two lineages of Puṣyabhūti and Mūkarava—resplendent with royal fortune for a long time, like the lunar and solar dynasties—have truly become united in their multitude of virtues that bring joy to the ears of the wise and are celebrated throughout the entire world.
Indeed, from the very beginning, you have stood in the heart of His Majesty like the Kaustubha gem by virtue of your qualities."
"But now you have become one who must be borne upon the head by the Supreme Lord, like the moon.
Even as he was speaking thus, the astrologers approached the king and said, "Your Majesty, the auspicious moment for the wedding is drawing near."
"Let the son-in-law go to the bridal chamber," they said.

Then, addressed by the king with the words, "Rise, go," Grahavarma entered the inner apartments and passed through the thousands of eyes of the women, who were eager to see their son-in-law, which fell upon him like groves of blooming blue water-lilies. He reached his destination.
He entered the door of the bridal chamber after having dismissed his attendants;
there he found her surrounded by a retinue consisting mostly of a few trusted dear friends, kinswomen, and young women.

With her face veiled by a garment as red as the dawn, she was like the morning twilight; by her own radiance, she rendered the lamps lusterless. She was embraced, yet not too tightly, by youth, as if apprehensive of her extreme delicacy.
With long, silent sighs released from a heart constricted by trepidation, she seemed to mourn the passing of her childhood.
Trembling violently, she was held motionless by shame, as if through fear of falling.
She was gazing at the moon, which was about to seize her hand— a hand that rivaled the red lotus— while her mind trembled with fear;
her slender body was white as sandalwood,
appearing as if born from the heart of a night-lily whose beauty had been gathered by the gift of moonlight.
She seemed to have emerged from the very heart of spring, wafting the fragrance of flowers; she appeared as if born from the Malaya breeze, which draws in swarms of bees by the scent of her breath;
she was like Rati herself, reborn after having followed Kāmadeva.

He beheld the bride, who was like a Goddess of Fortune fashioned by the ocean out of all the qualities of jewels—luster, loveliness, intoxication, fragrance, and sweetness—born respectively from the Kaustubha gem, the moon, wine, the Pārijāta tree, and nectar;
she seemed to dispel the melancholy shade of her eyes with her smooth cheek-surface, which was like a green meadow of emerald luster mingled with the white radiance of her pearl necklace;

and she appeared to reproach both her heart and her circle of friends, who were looking up with faces downcast, agitated by the curiosity to see the bridegroom, and repeatedly making efforts to lower their faces.
As soon as that thief of the heart entered, Kandarpa seized him while he was still bound and handed over;
and whatever was done by the women in the chamber of curiosity—with their laughing faces full of jesting and their playful gestures—he performed all of it with exceeding grace.

Taking the bride by the hand, who had assumed the attire appropriate for the wedding, he went out and proceeded to the slopes of the snowy mountain, which were white with fresh snow and filled with invited kings, like the slopes of the Himalayas summoned for the marriage of Tryambaka and Ambika.

Its perimeter was illuminated by five-faced water-pots—rough with the sprouts of young barley tender from the consecration—and by jars of various soft colors and by women with faces free of enemies, holding auspicious fruits in their hands and performing the añjali gesture;
there, twice-born observers were momentarily distracted as they watched the fire being kindled and smoking from the fuel being offered by the preceptors;
unblemished green kuśa grass was placed near the sacrificial fire, and a collection of stones, deerskins, clarified butter, ladles, and bundles of sacrificial wood was kept close at hand.
And he ascended that altar, which was smiling with parched grains mixed with dark leaves of the *śamī* tree placed upon a new winnowing basket,
just as the moon with its moonlight ascends the heavens;
and then he glided toward the fire, whose flickering, reddish shoots of flame were like the flower-armed god of love approaching a red *aśoka* tree accompanied by Rati.

And when the fire had been offered oblations, he circumambulated it clockwise along with the very flames—which, turning in a rightward spiral, seemed as if they were eager to gaze upon the face of the bride—while he himself moved in a clockwise direction.

As the handful of parched grain was being cast into the fire, the flame appeared as if smiling with wonder at the previously unseen beauty of the bride and groom, its body whitened by the rays from their fingernails.

In the meantime, she, suppressing any facial expression of distress, caused the reflection of the fire in the surface of her clear cheeks to seem like a dousing of the flames; meanwhile, a mass of large teardrops resembling pearls manifested a dark storm of grief.
The bride wept,

and a great wailing arose from the female relatives whose eyes were filled with tears. But when the series of marriage rites had been completed, the son-in-law bowed down before his father-in-law and mother-in-law along with the bride.
And he entered [the chamber], which was adorned on its door-panels with the image of Rati, the consort of the god of love;
which resounded with the humming of swarms of bees that had first entered as if out of affection;
and which was illuminated by auspicious lamps that were swaying in the breeze from the wings of the bee-swarms, as if trembling for fear of being struck by the lotuses at their ears.

It was presided over by the God of Love, who stood at the foot of a red *aśoka* tree in full bloom— its branches depicted in one corner— drawing an arrow with his strung bow, his three-eyed gaze cast askance;

it was graced by a couch adorned with a pillow and well-spread with rugs, attended on one side by a golden fly-whisk and on the other by a golden statuette holding an ivory fish-ornament, appearing like the Goddess Lakṣmī herself with a full-blown white lotus in her hand.

And he spent the night in that bedchamber, which was resplendent with a silver sleep-vase standing at the head of the bed—beautiful as a white water-lily and appearing like the moon come to aid the flower-armed god of love.
There, he watched the reflections of the new bride’s face in the jeweled walls and mirrors as she lay sleeping with her back turned in modesty;
these reflections appeared like the faces of the household deities who had arrived out of curiosity to overhear her first conversation, peering through the jeweled lattice windows.

Having stayed in his father-in-law’s household for ten days—which were filled with unique joys through ever-new attentions, as he showered nectar, as it were, upon his mother-in-law’s heart with his virtuous conduct—he was finally dismissed by the king with great difficulty. Like a royal gatekeeper leaving the palace, he left behind a lingering anxiety; and taking with him the hearts of all the people as if they were travel-provisions presented as part of her dowry, he departed for his own country together with his bride.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Birth of the Universal Monarch," in the *Harṣacarita* composed by the great poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa.
